pharm: NSAID / anti-inflammatory analgesic (active metabolite of phenylbutazone)
quick: Historically ~100 mg PO 3-4 times daily (300-600 mg/day)
Avoid - additive GI and CNS effects
Regular CBC; watch for sore throat, fever, bruising/bleeding
summary: Oxyphenbutazone is a pyrazolone NSAID and the principal active metabolite of phenylbutazone, with anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antipyretic activity used historically for rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout and other painful inflammatory conditions. It is NOT FDA-approved - systemic forms were withdrawn worldwide (around 1985, US brand Tandearil) chiefly because of life-threatening blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia). It also causes GI ulceration/bleeding, fluid retention, severe skin reactions and hepatotoxicity, and markedly potentiates oral anticoagulants. All systemic use is now considered obsolete.
indications: Osteoarthritis and other painful inflammatory conditions - tendinitis, bursitis, superficial thrombophlebitis (historical)

dosage.d: ~100 mg three to four times daily (about 300-600 mg/day)
dosage.n: Lowest effective dose for shortest period; systemic use now obsolete

dosage.d: Higher initial dose then taper per response

admin: Take oral doses with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal irritation
Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible duration
Stop immediately and check a blood count if sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, or bleeding/bruising occur
Avoid in children, the elderly, and pregnancy
moa: Oxyphenbutazone is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), reducing prostaglandin synthesis and thereby decreasing inflammation, pain and fever. It has a weak uricosuric effect at higher doses. It is the principal active metabolite of phenylbutazone.

absolute: Pre-existing blood dyscrasias or bone-marrow depression
Hypersensitivity to oxyphenbutazone, phenylbutazone or other pyrazolones
relative: Hypertension and congestive heart failure (fluid/sodium retention)
Children and the elderly (higher toxicity risk)
monitor: Concurrent sulfonylureas, phenytoin, methotrexate or lithium

lact: Avoid during breastfeeding - oxyphenbutazone is excreted in breast milk.
renal: Contraindicated or to be used only with great caution in renal impairment; it promotes sodium and fluid retention. Use caution in cardiac and renal disease.
hepatic: Contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment; hepatotoxicity can occur. The drug is hepatically metabolized.

major: Oral anticoagulants (warfarin/coumarins) - markedly potentiated with serious hemorrhage risk (protein-binding displacement plus inhibited metabolism)
moderate: Other NSAIDs - additive GI and renal toxicity
minor: Barbiturates, rifampicin, corticosteroids, promethazine, chlorpheniramine - may reduce oxyphenbutazone efficacy
interactions.food: Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal irritation.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive gastrointestinal injury and psychomotor impairment.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause leukopenia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver tests; can mask fever as an antipyretic.

monitoring: Regular complete blood counts (CBC) are essential
Clinical watch for sore throat, fever, oral ulceration, and bleeding/bruising as early signs of blood dyscrasia - discontinue immediately if suspected
Signs of GI bleeding (melena, abdominal pain)
Liver function, renal function and fluid status / blood pressure
counsel: Report immediately any sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, or unusual bruising or bleeding - these may signal a serious blood disorder
Report black or tarry stools or stomach pain (gastrointestinal bleeding)
Take with food; use only for as short a time as directed
Tell your clinician if you take a blood thinner, a diabetes medicine, or phenytoin
Report any blistering rash or skin peeling immediately
pk: Prolonged owing to long half-life; favors accumulation
Store in a cool, dry place protected from light
pearls: NOT FDA-approved - systemic forms withdrawn worldwide (~1985, US brand Tandearil) due to agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia
Blood dyscrasias can occur within weeks, may be irreversible or fatal - the defining hazard mandating CBC monitoring and patient warning about sore throat/fever/bleeding
Very long half-life (~72 h) and high protein binding (>95%) favor accumulation
Markedly potentiates warfarin/coumarin anticoagulants - serious bleeding risk
missed: Historical guidance: take the missed dose when remembered; if it is near the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Management is symptomatic and supportive, with attention to gastrointestinal, central nervous system, hepatic, renal and hematologic effects, and monitoring of blood counts.
